papers.title: A unified cross-scale framework for the dynamic Waddington landscape
papers.abstract: The Waddington epigenetic landscape is a foundational concept in developmental biology, yet its quantitative formulations remain largely disconnected from the population dynamics that originally motivated the metaphor. Existing approaches typically describe either intracellular gene-regulatory dynamics or population-level cell kinetics, but rarely both within a unified framework. Here, we develop a unified PDE-integral framework that couples stochastic gene-regulatory dynamics with probability-conserving population renewal, yielding a dynamic Waddington landscape $U(\vec{x}, t) = -\log f(\vec{x}, t)$ defined directly from the evolving epigenetic probability density $f(\vec{x}, t)$. Rigorous mathematical analysis of this framework establishes its well-posedness and provides conditions for the existence and uniqueness of stationary solutions. Application to canonical gene regulatory circuits shows that proliferation is not merely a determinant of population size, but an active regulator of landscape topology. Population renewal reshapes attractor stability and transition barriers in a circuit-dependent manner, generating transient plasticity in some regulatory architectures while stabilizing progenitor states in others. Under highly proliferative conditions, these interactions further produce oscillatory ``breathing'' landscapes. Together, these results establish population renewal as an integral component of cell-fate regulation and extend the Waddington landscape from a static description of intracellular dynamics to a predictive multiscale framework linking gene regulation, cell-state dynamics, and tissue homeostasis.

papers.title: Motility-induced phase separation drives aggregation in chemotactic systems
papers.abstract: We present a unified continuum framework that combines chemotactic feedback with motility-induced phase separation (MIPS) to investigate the physical origin of aggregation in self-secreting cell populations. While classical Keller-Segel theory attributes pattern formation to chemotactic instabilities, we show that this mechanism breaks down in systems with proportional density-dependent (autocrine) production and uptake: linear stability analysis reveals that chemical fluctuations decouple from density, eliminating chemotactic aggregation at leading order. In contrast, introducing density-dependent motility restores instability through a purely mechanical mechanism corresponding to MIPS. Our results demonstrate that chemotactic feedback does not alter the nature of this instability, but instead enhances its growth rate and accelerates aggregation. This unifies two central paradigms of biological self-organization and revises the role of chemotaxis in collective cell migration.

papers.title: Cell Migration Boundary Motion in Drosophila Egg Chambers: A Combined Phase Field and Chemoattractant Model
papers.abstract: In the Drosophila melanogaster egg chamber, collective migration of border cells toward the oocyte is guided by spatial chemoattractant gradients, yet the distribution of these signals within the tissue remains difficult to quantify experimentally. We develop a spatially resolved mathematical framework to examine how tissue geometry shapes local chemoattractant concentrations during migration. A phase-field model represents the egg chamber architecture and is coupled to a diffusion--reaction equation with spatially heterogeneous diffusivity, restricting free chemoattractant transport primarily to extracellular space while reducing diffusion within cellular domains. Chemoattractant is secreted from the oocyte boundary and degraded throughout the domain, producing geometry-dependent concentration patterns. We further couple this chemical field to a mechanical model of cluster migration through the Tangential Interface Migration (TIM) force, which links local chemoattractant cues with contact-mediated motion along neighboring nurse-cell interfaces. Simulations show that tissue architecture and signal localization jointly influence migration speed and directional persistence. In particular, geometric bottlenecks and intersections can flatten local gradients and slow migration. This framework provides a mechanistic approach for investigating how extracellular geometry, chemical signaling, and cell--cell interactions together regulate collective cell migration in vivo.

papers.title: A Phase-field Model for Apoptotic Cell Death
papers.abstract: The process of programmed cell death, namely apoptosis, is a natural mechanism that regulates healthy tissue, multicellular structures, and homeostasis. An improved understanding of apoptosis can significantly enhance our knowledge of biological processes and systems. For instance, pathogens can manipulate the apoptotic process to either evade immune detection or to facilitate their spread. Furthermore, of particular clinical interest is the ability of cancer cells to evade apoptosis, hence allowing them to survive and proliferate uncontrollably. Thus, in this work, we propose a phase-field framework for simulating intrinsic or extrinsic apoptosis induced by a cytotoxic phase, including deriving the configurational mechanics underlying such phenomena. The homogeneous analysis identifies degradation and recovery regimes under a fixed and evolving cytotoxic phase. To showcase model capabilities, we present simulations exhibiting different types of cellular dynamics produced when varying the mechanisms underlying apoptosis. The model is subsequently applied to probe different morphological transitions, such as cell shrinkage, membrane blebbing, cavity formation and fragmentation. Lastly, we compare the characteristics observed in our simulations to electron microscopy images, providing additional support for the model.
